doc.title: Vince DiMartino interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 8, 2025

title: Worst gigs: 50 Acres and Pilgrim State Hospital
summary: Asked about bizarre gigs, he tells of a depressing job with elderly players in Rochester and playing a veterans' show at Pilgrim State.

story.theme_name: Band pranks, jokes and gigs gone wrong
story.community_name: Pranks, practical jokes and band humor

blocks.x: Yeah. Well we’ve been at this for about an hour, and I wanted to fit in one last —
Whatever. Whatever you want to do is fine. I can talk all day, as you know. Go ahead.

Sometimes this is hard to remember, but in your lengthy career, can you recall — I’m going to use a couple of adjectives here. The most bizarre gig, the worst gig, the kind of gig you come home and tell your wife, you go, “You can’t believe what happened on this one.”

Most of them are — some of them are funny you know. Like one of them was the most depressing job for me personally okay? I get called, once again somebody was sick. It was in Rochester when I was a student. Somebody is sick and this guy calls up and says, “Can you come and play over at the 50 Acres” which was the big barn-like place you know what I mean? And they had weddings and different kinds of things, just like the first job I ever played. And so I showed up and the guy that was running the job, he was about 85 and he played violin. And I noticed that Joe Benedetto, he was the Vice President of the Musicians Union, was playing. I said, “Oh, I know Joe, at least I know Joe.” You know? Because I didn’t — and everybody in that group was — except for Joe, he was about 55 at the time — was over 70. Everybody. And there was no book. Okay? So the guy says, “Thanks for coming. Do you know the ‘Black Hawk Waltz’?” I said, “No.” I knew a lot of tunes, and this went on. I think I knew one tune in the first set. And now the guy, he felt bad because he knew that all the tunes were really old you know and

the ones that I did know I could really play. And then of course I could play solos when he wanted me to play a solo, but I couldn’t play the melody ever. I’d say just — but you know I’d listen and then I sort of sometimes I could play like a part of the melody because I figured it out just like I did the first job. I used the same technique. And then Joe Benedetto, he was sitting right next to me. The saxophone player? He says he knew what was going on and he said to me, “Vince, I have only known two or three tunes and I’m 55.” You know and so, he knew, because I was like 19 or something like that you know. And it was great. But it was depressing because I couldn’t really contribute anything you know what I mean? I just was sitting there. As a matter of fact I think I told the guys, I said, “Look, I didn’t do very good tonight, you don’t really have to pay me, I really played only about five tunes that I knew and I played some solos and that’s all I did.” He says, “Oh no, you sounded very nice.” And that was it. I said, “Okay whatever,” I said, “I could use the money.” But that was a terribly depressing job. Another one that was right with my dad. See my dad was a tap dancer and he was in the American Legion and like I said, I played pretty well when I was 14, like I could play, if I could play like Bunny Berigan, I could play “I Can’t Get Started,” I could play “Hey There” down an octave from where Maynard Ferguson played it. And I mean I could play all these characters acting you know. And so they had a little group that would go out to the veterans’ homes, the, you know the mental hospitals and stuff, all the different kinds of things for veterans mostly you know what I mean, where they might be. And so we would go out. And we went to this one hospital, which is infamous actually, and it got closed up. Pilgrim State Hospital out on Long Island. It was a big expose, maybe 40, 50 years ago on the Pilgrim State, how horrible the conditions were and everything. So we’re in this place right, and we start playing. And when I play people were starting to like scream and stuff. I didn’t know where I was. And it was horrifying. And I was going, “Jeez I’m hurting these people, I don’t know what’s going on.” You know because they were reacting to the music. They liked it, because they told me later, they said, “No, no,” the people that ran the place, they said, “we haven’t had this much excitement out of the people.” But for me on the stage it was horrifying. Because I thought I was like hurting people. Because trumpet is not the softest instrument. I thought I was — you know because sometimes the band director would tell you to play softer you know. So that was it. And one of the most exhilarating times was when I realized that you know sometimes I had to play some really hard solos. And I was already teaching at U.K. but I played in Cincinnati Pops and a lot of the recordings I did you know and the solos I did with the orchestra, well they played them in Carnegie Hall so I got to play those solos with the Cincinnati Orchestra in Carnegie Hall which you know that’s a little more nerve wracking at first. So the first thing I had to play in Carnegie Hall with the Cincinnati Pops
